Concept 05

Distributed processing

The same Pipeline, run by several processes at once against different slices of the same data. Coordination is a lease on a row range; durability is Arrow IPC bytes in TiKV.

In one line
Many nodes, one pipeline, at-least-once per row range
You need
pcs-service with tikv-store and a reachable TiKV; add distributed-raft for a cluster
Read this if
One process is not enough, and you need work to survive a node dying halfway through a batch

The claim loop

DistributedRunner holds three things: a store, a Box<dyn PipelineRuntime> used as a template, and a RunnerConfig. Calling run(world_factory) starts a loop that claims work, runs the template against it, persists the result, and acknowledges. Then it goes back for more, until the store says there is nothing pending.

The claim is the whole mechanism. PartitionSource::claim_next_batch hands back a BatchClaim: a batch_id, a half-open Range<u32> of rows, a fresh claim_id, and a lease that expires at a wall-clock millisecond. Hold the lease and the range is yours. Lose it and somebody else gets the same rows.

claims, leases, coordination rows and Arrow IPC bytes

Two lease mechanisms keep the window narrow. Before the run, should_renew checks whether less than 30 % of the TTL (or ten seconds, whichever is smaller) remains, and renews if so. During the run a renewal task sits beside run_on_with_state in the same tokio::select!, renewing at TTL/3. If a renewal fails the select resolves on the renewal branch, the run is cancelled at its next await point, and the claim is released rather than acked. A runner never keeps working on a lease it has lost.

The same is true after the run. If the checkpoint write fails, or the accumulator save fails, or the state blob save fails, the runner calls release_claim and skips the ack. Nothing is acknowledged that could not be made durable.

The runner does not load your rows

world_factory is called once per claim and whatever it returns is what the pipeline sees. The runner never reads the master batch's Arrow IPC back out of the store. Registering the components and filling in the rows for claim.row_range is your closure's job. See examples/distributed_fulfillment/store.rs, which wraps the store to intercept claim_next_batch and stash the IPC where the factory can reach it.

Standalone and clustered

Both modes use the same two traits, the same runner and the same TiKV store. Clustering adds a PCS Raft node beside it, for membership and leadership only.

FeatureWhat it adds
distributed PartitionSource, CheckpointStore, DistributedRunner and CheckpointStrategy. The traits and the runner loop, with no store of their own.
tikv-store TikvSharedStore, which implements both traits over a raw TiKV client, plus TikvStateClient for configs, source cursors and processor priors. The only shared store PCS ships.
distributed-raft The PCS Raft node, on tikv/raft-rs: RaftRedbLogStore over a log-only redb file, ArrowRaftDriver, and the TCP peer transport.
service-cluster service plus distributed-raft: what the pcs-service binary needs to run mode "cluster" from a config file. Build it with tikv-store as well: cluster mode refuses to start without a store "tikv" block.

A claim is a compare-and-swap on one row-range key, so the store arbitrates by itself. No work is routed through the Raft leader and no node hands a batch to another. The Raft node contributes membership and an elected leader, reported by the three pcs_raft_* gauges.

Publishing work

A master batch is a registered chunk of Arrow IPC with an id, a component name, a schema version, and a row count. Runners never create batches; they consume them.

Rustfive arguments, in this order
store
    .register_master_batch(
        0,                         // batch_id: u64
        Order::name().to_string(), // component: String
        1,                         // schema_id: u32
        ipc_bytes,                 // Vec<u8>, an Arrow IPC stream
        900,                       // total_rows: u32
    )
    .await?;

Registration is what creates the work. register_master_batch writes the batch record, then splits 0..total_rows into fixed 512-row ranges (TIKV_ROWS_PER_RANGE) and writes each one as a pending key. A 900-row batch becomes two ranges, so two nodes can run it at once. Parallelism is a function of how many rows you register, not how many batches.

claim_next_batch scans batch keys in id order, then row-range keys in row order, and takes the first range still marked pending. Both key layouts use fixed-width hex, so byte order equals numeric order and the scan needs no sort. Two nodes reaching the same range race on one compare-and-swap; the loser skips to the next pending range rather than retrying.

Two caps apply. MAX_LOG_ENTRY_BYTES is 1024 * 1024: register_master_batch rejects an Arrow IPC payload that size or larger, and so does the runner's own stage checkpoint. The window accumulator and the processor state blob go through CheckpointStore::max_checkpoint_bytes instead, which the TiKV store raises to 4 MiB (TIKV_MAX_CHECKPOINT_BYTES).

Running one node

One process against one TiKV is a real deployment, not a toy, and it is the shortest path to seeing the loop work. Nothing else changes when a second node joins: it connects to the same TiKV under the same key prefix and starts claiming.

Rustfeatures = "distributed", "tikv-store"
use std::time::Duration;

use pcs_service::PcsResult;
use pcs_service::component::Component;
use pcs_service::dataset::Dataset;
use pcs_service::distributed::{TikvSharedStore, TikvStoreConfig};
use pcs_service::distributed::runner::{DistributedRunner, RunnerConfig};
use pcs_service::distributed::strategy::CheckpointStrategy;
use pcs_service::pipeline::Pipeline;

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> PcsResult<()> {
    // Every key this process writes sits under `key_prefix`. Two deployments
    // sharing one TiKV stay apart by picking different prefixes.
    let store = TikvSharedStore::connect(&TikvStoreConfig {
        pd_endpoints: vec!["127.0.0.1:2379".to_string()],
        key_prefix: "pcs".to_string(),
        timeout: Duration::from_secs(10),
        lease_ttl_millis: 90_000,
    })
    .await?;

    let (ipc_bytes, total_rows) = encode_orders_ipc()?;
    store
        .register_master_batch(0, Order::name().to_string(), 1, ipc_bytes, total_rows)
        .await?;

    // A template. Its own dataset, sources and sinks are never used: each
    // claim runs against whatever `world_factory` hands back.
    let template = Pipeline::builder("order-processor")
        .with::<Order>()
        .with_system(ValidateOrder)
        .with_system(PriceOrder)
        .build();

    let runner = DistributedRunner::new(
        store,
        Box::new(template),
        RunnerConfig {
            checkpoint_strategy: CheckpointStrategy::EveryStage,
            schema_id: 1,
            max_batches: None,
            ..Default::default()
        },
    );

    // Called once per claim. Register the components and load the rows here.
    let processed = runner.run(hydrate_partition).await?;
    println!("{processed} batches acked");
    Ok(())
}

run returns the number of batches it acked. It stops when claim_next_batch returns None, or when max_batches is reached. For a long-lived service use run_with_shutdown, which takes a CancellationToken and exits between batches without holding a lease.

Where state lives

A cluster node writes one file of its own and shares everything else. The raft log is local to each node and holds no application data. TiKV holds the work, the claims and the checkpoints, and every node reads the same copy.

membership and leadership application state

All three checkpoint kinds share one key space and one API. They are told apart by stage_idx, and the two reserved values sit far above any real stage index, which numbers from zero and stays in the dozens.

ConstantValuePayload
none 0 The whole partition Dataset, written by the runner after the run.
PROCESSOR_STATE_STAGE_SENTINEL u32::MAX - 1 Whatever run_on_with_state returned. Opaque to the host.
ACCUMULATOR_STAGE_SENTINEL u32::MAX The WindowAccumulator component alone, via write_component_ipc.
The stage checkpoint is write-only, and there is one of it

The runner calls run_on_with_state once per claim, since the runtime runs its own stages internally, then writes a single checkpoint at stage_idx = 0. Nothing reads it back: recovery re-runs the batch from the top rather than resuming mid-pipeline. Two consequences. CheckpointStrategy::EveryNStages(n) only ever fires for n == 1, because the sole call is should_checkpoint(0). And the checkpoint is an artefact for an operator or an external reader, not a resume point.

Wiring a cluster

A cluster node runs two things side by side: the store it shares with every other node, and a Raft driver that gives the cluster a membership and a leader. ArrowRaftDriver::start is async, takes the raft log path, and returns the handle plus the driver's task. Keep the task alive for the life of the process.

Rustfeatures = "distributed-raft", "tikv-store"
use std::collections::HashMap;

use pcs_service::distributed::TikvSharedStore;
use pcs_service::distributed::consensus::{ArrowRaftDriver, ArrowRaftDriverConfig};

let (handle, _driver_task) = ArrowRaftDriver::start(
    ArrowRaftDriverConfig {
        node_id: 1,
        listen_addr: "0.0.0.0:9001".parse().unwrap(),
        // "host:port" strings, resolved lazily at connect time, so Docker
        // service names work. An empty map auto-initialises a single node.
        peers: HashMap::from([
            (2, "pcs-2:9001".to_string()),
            (3, "pcs-3:9001".to_string()),
        ]),
        heartbeat_interval_ms: 50,
        election_timeout_ms: 300,
        // Compact the log every this many applied entries.
        snapshot_log_interval: 10_000,
    },
    data_dir.join("raft-log.redb"),      // the one file this node owns
)
.await?;

// `start` wires outbound connections only. Without this listener peers cannot
// deliver votes or heartbeats and no leader is ever elected.
let _tcp_server = handle.spawn_tcp_server("0.0.0.0:9001".parse().unwrap());

// The store is independent of the driver: the same endpoints and the same
// key prefix on every node.
let store = TikvSharedStore::connect(&tikv_config).await?;

From here the runner code is byte-for-byte the single-node code: same template, same RunnerConfig, same runner.run(...). Only the driver is new.

Membership is static. The driver seeds its conf state from the configured peers on first boot, so no node calls an initialize step and no node forwards work to another. bootstrap #true writes a bootstrap.lock that records the operator deliberately created this cluster; it does not elect anybody.

You do not route work to the leader, because there is nothing to route. claim_next_batch talks to TiKV on every node, and TiKV's own compare-and-swap decides who wins a contested range. The driver answers who is in the cluster and who leads it, which is what the three pcs_raft_* gauges report. The pcs-service binary does all of the wiring above from a config file under mode "cluster", so hand-rolling it is only for embedding the runner in your own process.

What refuses to start

Four refusals stand in front of a cluster node. Each one is an error at startup rather than a divergence later.

  • No store "tikv" block under mode "cluster": TiKV is the only cluster application-data store, so there is nothing to fall back to.
  • A store block in a binary built without the tikv-store feature. A section the binary cannot honour is a refusal, never an ignored key.
  • raft-log.redb in data_dir without bootstrap.lock, which means a process died before bootstrap finished.
  • A node-id file disagreeing with node.id, which means this data directory belongs to a different node.

One more gate runs once the store is connected. The node compares its runtime's Arrow schema fingerprint against the one recorded beside its checkpoints and refuses to resume on state of a different shape.

State that outlives a batch

A native Pipeline keeps everything it knows in the Dataset, so the default run_on_with_state ignores prior, delegates to run_on, and returns Ok(None). Nothing extra is persisted.

A WASM processor cannot do that. Every call gets a fresh wasmtime Store, so processor linear memory does not survive a batch. That is deliberate: a trapped instance cannot corrupt anything that outlives it. The one channel left is the return value:

Rustthe host seam, from pcs-core
async fn run_on_with_state(
    &self,
    data: &mut Dataset,
    prior: Option<&[u8]>,
) -> PcsResult<Option<Vec<u8>>>;

WasmPipelineRuntime passes prior straight into the processor's run-batch export and returns the checkpoint field of the result. The runner stores that blob under PROCESSOR_STATE_STAGE_SENTINEL and hands it back as the next call's prior. On the processor side, one macro form opts in:

Rustin the processor crate
// Stateless: `prior` is ignored, `checkpoint` is always None.
pcs_processor::export_pipeline!(build);

// Stateful: systems read and write a `ProcessorState<Counter>` resource, and
// whatever they leave in it becomes the next batch's `prior`.
pcs_processor::export_pipeline!(build, state = Counter);

The pointer to the newest blob is a chain, not a fixed key: the blob is written under the claim that produced it and read back under the id of the claim that wrote the previous one, because the store resolves a checkpoint's batch_id through the claim index and rejects a write whose uuid is not a live claim. Reads survive the ack, so the chain holds for as long as the runner loop does. A runner that restarts hands the runtime None, so the processor starts cold and rebuilds its state.
